query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In untreated (pre‐exposed) Q235 steel, the native thin iron oxide film provides effective corrosion protection at room temperature, but when the steel is exposed to an aggressive salt environment at 700–900 °C, thermal stresses and accelerated oxidation cause the oxide film to crack and spall. This breakdown exposes the underlying metal and accelerates corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel in its native pre‐exposure state, bearing its thin, naturally formed iron oxide film along with inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.intervention: Expose the as‐received Q235 steel to an aggressive salt environment under two controlled temperature regimes: room temperature versus high temperature (700–900 °C).
generation.conditions: Experiments are conducted with identical salt compositions and exposure durations. The room-temperature condition tests the performance of the intact oxide film under mild oxidation, while the high-temperature condition accelerates oxidation kinetics and imposes thermal expansion stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity, continuity, and adhesion of the native iron oxide film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature the native oxide remains intact, limiting ion transport and corrosion. Under high-temperature conditions, the differential thermal expansion between the oxide and the steel and rapid oxidation kinetics lead to cracking and spallation of the oxide. This destabilization reduces the passivating effect, thereby exposing fresh metal to corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel exposed to the aggressive salt at room temperature will show minimal mass change and low corrosion rates, whereas under 700–900 °C exposure, the samples will exhibit significant breakdown of the oxide layer, greater mass loss, and enhanced corrosion indicators.
generation.baseline: As-received Q235 steel samples kept in a non-aggressive or inert environment, where the native oxide film remains stable.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies to untreated Q235 steel with its naturally formed oxide film and under conditions where no additional protective coatings or alloying modifications are present. It is expected to be effective in environments where the salt is aggressive enough to promote thermal stresses, but may not hold if alternative stabilization of the oxide occurs.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of oxide film degradation (e.g., critical temperature or salt aggressiveness needed for spallation) and the exact kinetics of film breakdown are not fully established and warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of as‐received Q235 steel coupons. Expose one set to an aggressive salt environment at room temperature and a second set to the same salt environment at 700–900 °C for identical durations. Characterize the surface morphology and integrity of the oxide film using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Simultaneously, measure the mass change and assess corrosion rates using gravimetric and electrochemical methods.
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide integrity (SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed at 700–900 °C do not exhibit statistically significant degradation of the oxide film (e.g., fewer cracks, reduced spallation) or higher mass loss and corrosion rates compared to room-temperature samples, the hypothesis that high-temperature exposure destabilizes the protective oxide would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

Following the significant Mn dissolution from the alloy into the salt to form MnF2, the Mn/MnF2 redox couple could become a salt redox buffer, and thus the immersed sample, would then be fixed at this buffer level. At this potential, the Cr becomes a noble element with respect to the salt, and Cr dissolution would not be thermodynamically favorable. It is not known how much Mn in the salt is required to reach a satisfactory buffer level, but that would be an interesting point to study in the future. These observations point to the possibility of using Mn/MnF2 couple as a redox buffer to reduce the overall corrosion potential and to slow or stop the dissolution of Cr. Such technique, in principle, was employed in the MSR experiment in ORNL during the 1960s by adding metallic elements such as Mg, Zr, and Be to the salt,. However, in our case, the structural materials would provide a constant source of buffer to the salt. Another possible mechanism is that adding Mn to the alloy in molten salt environment could act as a sacrificial mechanism to protect the Cr content. drafts.hypothesis: In Q235 steel, controlled annealing prior to high‐temperature corrosion exposure promotes a more homogeneous microstructure that, during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, forms a dense and adherent oxide scale (potentially containing protective spinel phases) that better resists corrosion. In contrast, the as-received (unannealed) state—with its inherent microstructural heterogeneities and inclusions—leads to nonuniform, porous oxide scales that degrade protection.
drafts.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 steel with typical microstructural heterogeneities and inclusions.
drafts.intervention: A controlled annealing treatment (with specified temperature and duration) applied to Q235 steel prior to high‐temperature, salt-induced corrosion testing.
drafts.conditions: Testing should be conducted under aggressive salt exposure at high temperatures (700–900 °C) to trigger rapid oxidation; parallel assessments at room temperature serve as a control where the effect is expected to be minimal.
drafts.structural_mediator: Reduction in microstructural heterogeneities and inclusion density that otherwise act as preferential sites for nonuniform oxidation and scale defect formation.
drafts.mechanism: Annealing homogenizes the microstructure and mitigates the concentration of defect sites. This leads to the formation of a more uniform and adherent oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, whereas in the unannealed steel, localized defects facilitate non-protective, porous oxide growth that accelerates corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature, salt-exposed conditions, annealed Q235 steel will show a lower mass gain (or more limited mass change) and improved oxide scale integrity (as observed through SEM and XRD) compared to unannealed samples. At room temperature, both sample types will display minimal differences in corrosion behavior.
drafts.baseline: As-received (unannealed) Q235 steel tested under the same corrosive environmental conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesized mechanism is expected to dominate under high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C) with aggressive salt exposure. At room temperature, where oxidation kinetics are slower and less aggressive, the impact of annealing on corrosion behavior is predicted to be negligible.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel samples: one set subjected to a controlled annealing treatment and one kept as-received. Expose both groups to aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C and, separately, at room temperature as a control. Characterize the resulting oxide scales using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) for structural integrity and phase composition. Measure mass change over time and perform electrochemical tests to evaluate corrosion rates.
measurements: SEM imaging of oxide scale morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide scale uniformity, lower mass change, or improved corrosion resistance relative to unannealed samples under 700–900 °C salt exposure, or if similar differences are observed under room-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In pre-exposed Q235 steel, a uniform, compact nanocrystalline iron oxide layer forms naturally during high‐temperature salt exposure, creating a diffusion barrier that retards further corrosion. In contrast, at room temperature, the oxide formation remains incomplete and defective, leading to enhanced corrosion degradation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its native, pre-exposure state with its as-produced microstructure and the initial thin, naturally formed oxide layer.
drafts.intervention: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set with the pristine native oxide layer intact and another set from which the oxide layer has been mechanically/chemically removed. Expose both sets to controlled environments – one at high-temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt (e.g., NaCl) exposure and one at room-temperature salt exposure.
drafts.conditions: Experiments are conducted under well-controlled thermal conditions: a high-temperature regime (e.g., 800 °C) where oxide layer evolution is enhanced, and a room-temperature environment where oxide development is minimal. The intervention involving oxide removal is only applied at the initial stage prior to exposure.
drafts.structural_mediator: The structure, thickness, and nano-scale uniformity of the in situ–formed iron oxide scale (likely a mixture of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3) that acts as a physical barrier to aggressive species.
drafts.mechanism: At high temperatures, the native oxide on Q235 steel rapidly evolves into a dense, adherent, and nanocrystalline scale that impedes ion diffusion and oxygen ingress, thereby mitigating corrosion (as observed in analogous stainless and alloy steels). At room temperature, insufficient thermal energy prevents full transformation or healing of defects in the oxide, resulting in a more porous layer that fails to provide effective protection.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature salt exposure, samples retaining the native oxide will exhibit reduced mass change, maintained or improved hardness, and a more coherent oxide microstructure relative to oxide-stripped samples. Under room-temperature conditions, the protective effects are diminished in both sample sets, with the stripped samples showing accelerated corrosion compared to any marginal benefit from an incomplete oxide in intact samples.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel samples with the native oxide layer maintained, exposed under standard ambient conditions with no additional oxide removal intervention.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is hypothesized for Q235 steel in its unalloyed, pre-exposure state. It may not extend to steels with significant alloying elements or those that have undergone prior thermal treatments that change oxide scale formation dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel samples: one with the native oxide layer intact and one with the oxide layer removed via a controlled chemical/mechanical process. Expose subsets of both groups to a high-temperature environment (e.g., 800 °C with a standardized NaCl deposit) and to a room-temperature environment with similar salt conditions. After a fixed exposure time, conduct measurements of mass change, hardness, and oxide layer microstructure using SEM and XRD.
measurements: Mass change (weight gain/loss) pre- and post-exposure
Microstructural analysis (SEM imaging for oxide layer morphology, XRD for phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under high-temperature salt exposure conditions, samples with the intact native oxide do not show statistically significant improvements in mass change, hardness, and oxide scale coherence compared to the oxide-stripped samples, then the hypothesis would be falsified. Similarly, if room-temperature exposures reveal no differences in degradation between samples with and without the native oxide, it would contradict the predicted temperature-dependent protective mechanism.

drafts.hypothesis: For as-received Q235 steel, the native thin iron oxide layer acts as a passive barrier at room temperature, but when exposed to aggressive salt environments at 700–900 °C, thermal stresses and microstructural changes lead to the breakdown and spallation of this protective film, exposing the metal to accelerated corrosion.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure (as-received) state with its native, thin, and relatively intact iron oxide film.
drafts.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to two sets of conditions: room temperature in a controlled saline environment versus high temperature (700–900 °C) in a molten salt (or similarly aggressive salt vapor) environment. In one set, optionally pre-anneal samples in air to further form or modify the native oxide, and compare to untreated samples.
drafts.conditions: The hypothesis applies when the steel is exposed to an aggressive salt medium. At room temperature, the passive film remains largely intact. At high temperatures, thermal expansion mismatch and changes in oxide composition and adhesion cause film breakdown. It would not apply if the oxide film is artificially stabilized (e.g., via alloying or protective coatings) or if the salt environment is not aggressive (e.g., inert atmospheres).
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity (or breakdown) of the native passive iron oxide layer (and its coherence and adhesion to the substrate).
drafts.mechanism: At room temperature, the native Fe-oxide film forms a continuous barrier that limits ion transport and corrosion. Under high-temperature salt exposure, differences in thermal expansion and possible phase transformations induce cracking or spallation of the oxide film, thereby exposing the underlying metal to the corrosive salt, which accelerates degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under room-temperature exposure, minimal mass change and low corrosion rate will be observed due to the intact passive film. In contrast, high-temperature exposure will show significant mass loss, evidence of oxide film breakdown (e.g., cracks or spalled regions), and localized attack at grain boundaries where the oxide film has failed.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel samples held in an inert or non-aggressive environment at room temperature that maintain the intact oxide film.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to govern corrosion behavior in low-alloy steels with similar composition and native oxide films. It may not apply if external oxidation inhibitors, protective alloying elements, coatings, or treatments are present that modify the formation or stability of the oxide layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several Q235 steel coupons in the as-received state. Subject one group to a room-temperature saline exposure and another group to 700–900 °C molten salt exposure for a fixed duration. Characterize the surface before and after exposure using SEM, XRD, and mass loss measurements. Optionally, include a subset with a pre-formed enhanced oxide layer for comparison.
measurements: SEM imaging and cross-sectional analysis of oxide film integrity
XRD phase analysis of oxide and substrate
Surface roughness and adhesion testing of the oxide film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature exposure in the aggressive salt environment does not lead to significant deterioration of the oxide layer (i.e., no observable cracks, spallation, or increased corrosion rate compared to room-temperature conditions), then the hypothesis that film breakdown controls accelerated high-temperature corrosion would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The corrosion protection of pre‐exposed Q235 steel is governed by its native, thin iron oxide layer, which at room temperature forms a continuous, adherent film that limits further oxidation, but under high‐temperature aggressive salt exposure (700–900 °C) this oxide layer is destabilized (by accelerated oxidation/dissolution and spallation) leading to rapid exposure and degradation of the underlying metal.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with its native, thin iron oxide film and minimal alloying elements.
drafts.intervention: Expose the Q235 steel samples to an aggressive salt environment (e.g., a Na2SO4–NaCl mixture) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures of 700–900 °C without any additional surface treatments.
drafts.conditions: The hypothesis applies under similar salt compositions, exposure durations, and atmospheric conditions; it is expected to hold for untreated Q235 steel but may not apply if additional protective coatings or alloying modifications are present.
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity, continuity, and adhesion of the native iron oxide layer on the steel surface.
drafts.mechanism: At room temperature, the modest oxidation leads to formation of a stable, continuous iron oxide layer that passivates the surface. At high temperatures, however, the molten salt environment accelerates chemical reactions, causing the oxide to dissolve or spall off. This exposes fresh metal to oxidative attack, thereby increasing the corrosion rate and mass loss.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under room-temperature conditions, Q235 steel will show low corrosion rates and minimal mass change due to the retained protective oxide. In contrast, when exposed to salt at 700–900 °C, there will be significant mass loss and observable breakdown or alteration of the oxide layer, leading to accelerated corrosion.
drafts.baseline: Measurements of corrosion rates (and mass change) for Q235 steel in inert or non-salt environments at both room temperature and high temperatures would be significantly lower than those in the salt (aggressive) conditions, highlighting the role of the salt–temperature interplay in disrupting the oxide layer.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is specific to unmodified Q235 steel with its native oxide film. It may not apply to steels with engineered alloying (e.g., stainless steels) or added corrosion inhibitors that form more robust passivation layers.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several Q235 steel samples in their as-received state and subject them to three conditions: (a) room-temperature immersion in a Na2SO4–NaCl salt solution, (b) high-temperature (700–900 °C) exposure to molten salt under controlled conditions, and (c) an inert environment (control) at both temperatures. Pre- and post-exposure, characterize the oxide layer using SEM, EDS, and XRD, and quantify mass loss and corrosion rates via gravimetric analysis and electrochemical measurements.
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide integrity (SEM imaging)
Oxide composition and phase identification (EDS and XRD)
Corrosion rate (potentiodynamic polarization or other electrochemical methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature salt exposure does not lead to a significant breakdown or alteration of the native oxide (i.e., if surface oxide integrity, mass loss, and corrosion rates remain similar to room-temperature or inert conditions), then the hypothesis that the destabilization of the native oxide under molten salt conditions is responsible for accelerated corrosion would be falsified.
